newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: U.S.'s Albright visits a Guatemala at peace.
newsitem.headline: U.S.'s Albright visits a Guatemala at peace.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrived in Guatemala on Sunday for a one-day visit to lend U.S. support to the country's fledgling era of peace following 36 years of civil war.

Foreign Relations Minister Eduardo Stein met Albright at a Guatemala City Air Force base and then escorted her on a U.S. military Blackhawk helicopter to a guerrilla disarmament camp where former leftist rebels recently turned in their weapons.

Albright was expected to briefly visit the Tululche camp, some 40 miles (70 km) north of Guatemala City, before meeting with President Alvaro Arzu at his private ranch in southern Guatemala and flying to Mexico later in the day.

Stein said Albright's visit to this impoverished Central American nation was a sign the United States was interested in helping Guatemala keep its hard-fought peace after supporting the government's counter-insurgency efforts for decades.

The United States has promised $40 million a year for the next four years to help Guatemala pay for the costs of implementing peace accords signed between the government and Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit rebels on Dec. 29.
"We see it as a new and very special sign of the (U.S.) government's interest in the peace process in which they have collaborated," Stein told reporters at the airport before Albright's arrival.

During the 1970s and 1980s the United States poured funds into the Guatemalan army, but aid was cut off in 1990 after the Congress began to look into the army's hideous human rights record. The war claimed some 100,000 lives.

A centrist businessman, Arzu took power in January, 1996 and by year's end had carried out his campaign pledge to end the civil war. Total pledges of aid for peace from a long list of international donors reaches more than $1.9 billion.

Stein said Albright and Arzu would discuss bilateral issues of trade, security and justice, sustainable development and immigration, issues also expected to be the central topics at a May 8 summit in Costa Rica between Clinton and his Central American counterparts.

Later in the day, Albright was scheduled to fly to Mexico to join President Clinton during his three-day visit to that nation. Albright and Stein were also expected to sign an agreement on coordinating efforts to fight auto theft.
